title: Mixture-Dependent Toxicity of E-Cigarette Constituents: Cytotoxicity, Inflammation, and DNA-Repair-Associated Protein Responses in Bronchial Epithelial Cells
content: Electronic cigarette aerosols contain complex mixtures of flavoring chemicals and metals released from device components, yet the biological effects of these constituents in combination remain poorly understood. We examined the effects of vanillin, WS23, ethyl vanillin, p-anisaldehyde, and nickel oxide (NiO), alone and in selected mixtures at different ratios, in BEAS-2B human bronchial epithelial cells. Each flavoring chemical reduced metabolic activity and cellular ATP in a concentration-dependent manner. Chou–Talalay analysis showed synergistic interactions between vanillin and WS23 (combination index (CI) < 1) and antagonistic interactions between ethyl vanillin and p-anisaldehyde (CI > 1). Ethyl vanillin (100 µM), NiO (50 µg/cm²), and their combination did not significantly reduce cell viability but were associated with increased interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) in conditioned medium. Total H2AX abundance was unchanged by aldehyde-metal combinations. However, endonuclease VIII-like 2 (NEIL2) showed nonsignificant increases following NiO and combined exposure, whereas polynucleotide kinase 3′-phosphatase (PNKP) increased significantly following ethyl vanillin and combined ethyl vanillin–NiO exposure, suggesting the base-excision repair (BER) pathway mitigating oxidative damage. We show that e-cigarette constituents at relevant concentrations as a mixture may induce oxidative damage but can be repaired by BER. These findings demonstrate that e-cigarette constituents can produce mixture-dependent responses that are not predicted by individual exposures and the inflammatory and DNA-repair-associated responses observed under noncytotoxic conditions warrant further investigation.
